title: Antigen Tests: What a Negative Result Does and Does Not Rule Out
summary: Interpret rapid strep, Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigen, and cryptococcal antigen tests by their sensitivity, target and timing, and know which follow-up test to send after a negative.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 66 Hits 6, 11 and 13 and Traps 2, 3 and 6. Checked against Baron 2013 (IDSA/ASM laboratory utilization guide), Kim 2022 and Bouzid 2021. Not taught: “collect two throat swabs,” “sensitivity as low as 70%” (Bouzid 2021 lists 75–85% for two lateral-flow assays), and “India ink poor except in HIV” — not stated in the sources read. The 2018 IDSA/ASM update was read only as an abstract.

objectives: Explain how sensitivity, target and timing determine what a negative test means.
Interpret rapid strep antigen results in children and adults.
State the target and limitations of Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigen tests.
Choose cryptococcal antigen over India ink and select follow-up tests after a negative antigen result.

scenes.title: Three negative antigen tests
scenes.altText: Three cards. Card A: a 7-year-old with fever and exudative tonsillitis; rapid strep antigen negative. Card B: a returning traveller with severe pneumonia; Legionella urinary antigen negative. Card C: a man with HIV, headache and fever; CSF India ink negative, cryptococcal antigen not yet sent. A question token: “Which negatives can you trust?” The cartoon scientist holds three negative cassettes.

cues.text: A seven-year-old with fever and pus on the tonsils has a negative rapid strep antigen test.
A traveller with severe pneumonia has a negative Legionella urinary antigen.
A man with HIV and headache has a negative India ink stain on his spinal fluid. Three negatives. Which of them can you trust?

scenes.title: What a negative result actually means
scenes.altText: A probability bar (schematic): a negative test lowers the chance of disease, by how much depends on sensitivity and on what the test targets. Three cards: sensitivity (how many true cases test positive), target (which organism or antigen the assay detects), timing (antigen present or not yet / no longer). A note: a highly specific test with modest sensitivity is better at ruling in than ruling out.

cues.text: A negative result is not a verdict; it lowers the probability of disease. How far it lowers it depends on three things.
First, sensitivity: what share of true cases the test detects. A test that misses one case in four leaves real doubt after a negative.
Second, the target: which organism, species or antigen the assay is built to detect. Anything outside the target will always be negative.
Third, timing and specimen: whether enough antigen was present in that sample at that moment.
A highly specific test with modest sensitivity is good at ruling disease in, and weak at ruling it out.

props.label: Specific but insensitive → good to rule in, weak to rule out

scenes.title: Three tests, three different blind spots
scenes.altText: Three test cards. Rapid strep antigen (lateral flow): sensitivities around 75–85% in one review, specificity ~96–98%; professional societies agree that negative rapid tests in children should be confirmed by culture or a molecular assay; generally not needed for adults. Legionella urinary antigen: detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1 only — 80–95% of community legionellosis in the US and Europe but only ~50% in Australia/New Zealand; antigen can persist for weeks to months (60+ days in ~10% in one study); culture on BCYE remains the gold standard. Cryptococcal antigen: has replaced India ink for rapid diagnosis; > 90% sensitivity and specificity; most sensitive on CSF.

cues.text: Rapid strep antigen tests are specific, but their sensitivity runs around 75 to 85 percent in one review. That is why a negative test in a child should be confirmed by culture or a molecular test; in adults it is generally not needed.
The Legionella urinary antigen detects only Legionella pneumophila serogroup 1.

That serogroup causes 80 to 95 percent of community legionellosis in the US and Europe, but only about half in Australia and New Zealand. Other serogroups and species test negative. Culture on BCYE agar remains the gold standard.
And the antigen can linger for weeks to months, so a positive result may reflect a recent, not a current, infection.
For cryptococcal meningitis, the cryptococcal antigen test has replaced India ink. Its sensitivity and specificity exceed 90 percent, and it is most sensitive on spinal fluid.

scenes.title: Pneumococcal urinary antigen and what to send next
scenes.altText: A pneumococcal urinary antigen card: pooled sensitivity ~75%, specificity ~95%; false positives after a pneumonia within the previous 3 months, in colonized children with chronic lung disease, and within 48 hours of pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine. A next-step board: A (child, rapid strep −) → throat culture or NAAT; B (traveller, Legionella antigen −) → lower-respiratory culture on BCYE and/or NAAT; C (HIV, India ink −) → CSF cryptococcal antigen. A footer: antigen tests do not provide isolates for susceptibility testing or outbreak typing.

cues.text: The pneumococcal urinary antigen has a pooled sensitivity of about 75 percent and specificity of about 95 percent.
It can stay positive after a pneumonia in the previous three months, in children colonized with pneumococcus who have chronic lung disease, and for 48 hours after the polysaccharide vaccine.
So for patient A, send a throat culture or a molecular test.
For patient B, send lower-respiratory secretions for Legionella culture on BCYE agar or a nucleic acid test, which can detect other serogroups and species.
For patient C, send a cryptococcal antigen on the spinal fluid. And remember: antigen tests give no isolate for susceptibility testing or outbreak typing.

props.label: No isolate → no susceptibility, no outbreak typing

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Child with negative rapid strep — no further testing” (✓ confirm with culture or NAAT); “Negative Legionella urinary antigen rules out Legionnaires’ disease” (✓ detects serogroup 1 only — culture/NAAT); “Negative India ink rules out cryptococcal meningitis” (✓ cryptococcal antigen has replaced it).

cues.text: Trap one: a child with a negative rapid strep test needs nothing more. Confirm with a culture or a molecular test.
Trap two: a negative Legionella urinary antigen rules out Legionnaires’ disease. It detects serogroup 1 only. Send culture or a nucleic acid test.
Trap three: a negative India ink rules out cryptococcal meningitis. The cryptococcal antigen test has replaced it.

scenes.title: Know the net before you trust the empty catch
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Know the net before you trust the empty catch.” A fishing-net token: small holes (sensitivity) and a narrow mouth (target). A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: know the net before you trust the empty catch. A net with big holes, low sensitivity, or a narrow mouth, a single target, can come up empty while the fish is there.
Where it breaks: performance varies by brand and population; a positive can also mislead, as with lingering Legionella antigen; and molecular tests have their own limits.

props.title: Where it breaks
lines: Performance varies by brand and population

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Rapid strep − in a child → culture/NAAT · Legionella urine Ag = SG1 only · CrAg replaced India ink”, “Pneumococcal urine Ag: sens ~75%, false + after recent CAP, colonized children, PPSV ≤ 48 h”.

cues.text: Before trusting a negative antigen test, know its sensitivity and its target: confirm negative strep tests in children, remember Legionella antigen sees serogroup 1 only, and use cryptococcal antigen instead of India ink.

props.label: Child strep Ag − → culture/NAAT · Legionella Ag = SG1 only · CrAg > India ink
Pneumococcal urine Ag: sens ~75% · false + recent CAP, colonized kids, PPSV ≤ 48 h

explanation.what: Plain language: rapid antigen tests look for a piece of one organism; a negative result can mean the organism is absent, too scarce, or simply not the kind the test looks for. Scientific terms: sensitivity, specificity, lateral-flow immunoassay, rapid antigen detection test (RADT), urinary antigen test (UAT), L. pneumophila serogroup 1, cryptococcal capsular polysaccharide antigen (CrAg), BCYE agar.
explanation.why: Antigen tests detect a defined epitope; organisms or serogroups lacking it test negative. Antigen quantity varies with specimen and timing; some antigens persist after recovery. High specificity with moderate sensitivity favours ruling in over ruling out.
explanation.measure: Rapid strep lateral flow: ~75–85% sensitive, ~96–98% specific (two assays, Bouzid 2021); confirm negatives in children by culture or NAAT. Legionella UAT: L. pneumophila SG1 only (80–95% of community cases US/Europe, ~50% Australia/NZ); antigen persists weeks–months. Pneumococcal UAT: pooled sensitivity 75%, specificity 95%. CrAg: > 90% sensitivity and specificity; most sensitive on CSF.
explanation.differs: Rule-in tests (specific) vs rule-out tests (sensitive). Antigen tests (no isolate) vs culture (isolate for susceptibility and typing). Legionella UAT (SG1) vs culture/NAAT (broader).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: backup testing after a negative pediatric rapid strep, Legionella UAT limited to serogroup 1, CrAg replacing India ink, and false-positive pneumococcal antigen scenarios.

comparisons.title: Legionella urinary antigen vs culture
comparisons.distinguisher: Target breadth and whether an isolate is obtained.

mnemonic.text: Know the net before you trust the empty catch.
mnemonic.explanation: A test’s sensitivity (the holes) and target (the mouth) decide whether an empty result means no organism.
mnemonic.limitation: Performance varies by brand and population; positives can also mislead (lingering antigen); molecular tests have their own limits.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old with fever, tonsillar exudate and tender cervical nodes has a negative rapid strep antigen test. What should the laboratory recommend?

options.text: Confirm with a throat culture or molecular assay
options.rationale: Correct. Professional societies agree negative rapid antigen tests in children should be confirmed.
Incorrect. Rapid antigen tests miss a meaningful share of true infections.

options.text: Repeat the same rapid test in 1 hour
options.rationale: Incorrect. Repeating the same insensitive test does not resolve the doubt.
Incorrect. Culture or a molecular test is the recommended confirmation for a negative rapid test.

questions.stem: A patient in Australia has severe community-acquired pneumonia; Legionella urinary antigen is negative. What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Legionellosis is not excluded; the test detects only L. pneumophila serogroup 1, so send culture or NAAT
options.rationale: Correct. In Australia/NZ only about half of cases are serogroup 1, and other species are missed.
Incorrect. Non-SG1 serogroups and other species test negative.

options.text: Repeat the urine antigen weekly until positive
options.rationale: Incorrect. A test that cannot detect the organism will stay negative.

options.text: Send a pneumococcal urinary antigen instead
options.rationale: Incorrect. That tests for a different organism.

questions.stem: Which result is most consistent with a false-positive pneumococcal urinary antigen?

options.text: Positive antigen 24 hours after pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccination
options.rationale: Correct. Recent polysaccharide vaccine (within 48 h) can cause false positives.

options.text: Positive antigen with S. pneumoniae in blood culture
options.rationale: Incorrect. This is a true positive.
Incorrect. That is a true negative for pneumococcus.

options.text: Positive antigen in a previously healthy adult with lobar pneumonia
options.rationale: Incorrect. That is a plausible true positive.
